name: Southern Bobo Madaré
catalog_citation: Sherwood, Kate. 2016. Intonational phrase boundaries in Southern Bobo Madaré. Proceedings of Speech Prosody 2016 (Boston, 31 May-3 June 2016), 89-93. doi:10.21437/SpeechProsody.2016-19 (open access, ISCA archive)
catalog_locator: p. 89, sec. 1.1 'Tone in Southern Bobo Madaré' (right column); saved file, PDF p. 1
catalog_quote: Bobo is a lexical tone language with a complex tone system. There are three lexical tone levels: high (H), mid (M), and low (L). Bobo also has contour tones. Morse [7] claims LM, LH, and ML contour tones, which she analyzes as a sequence of level tones sharing the same domain (the syllable). Le Bris and Prost [8] claim that the contour tones are LH, MH, HL, and ML. Because the number and identity of the contour tones is uncertain, phrases in which contour tones were in positions critical to the analysis were excluded in analysis of F0 this study. In addition to lexical tone, Bobo has grammatical tone. This has some implications for the data used in this project. According to Le Bris and Prost [8], the perfect of transitive verbs is marked with grammatical low tone.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Bobo is described as a three-level lexical tone language (H, M, L) with contour tones and grammatical tone; no source opened says anything about word stress or accent placement. Corroborated by Dienst 2004: 6 'BObO ist eine Tonsprache mit drei Tonhöhen. Ein Vokal kann Träger von zwei Tönen sein.' (Bobo is a tone language with three pitch levels; a vowel can carry two tones.)
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; Sherwood notes that the contour-tone inventory differs between Morse 1976 and Le Bris & Prost 1981, and that perfective verbs carry grammatical L tone.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level lexical tone plus phrase-level boundary tones (Sherwood's study is about intonational-phrase boundaries, elicited sentences and conversation from 3 speakers in Bobo-Dioulasso). Stress is simply not discussed; the two primary phonological descriptions (Morse 1976; Sanou 1978) and the Le Bris & Prost 1981 grammatical introduction could not be opened and might contain an explicit accent statement.
new_statements.identity_note: Both opened sources describe the Southern dialect of Bobo-Dioulasso (Sherwood: 3 speakers recorded in Bobo-Dioulasso; Dienst: data from Morse 1976 and Le Bris & Prost 1981, dialect of Bobo-Dioulasso = Sya/Syabéré area; Glottolog dialects syaa1239/syab1238 under sout2840). Northern Bobo (Tansila; Prost 1983) is a separate Glottolog language (bbo) and was not used. Wikipedia and Ethnologue treat both under 'Bobo' (bobo1253 family node).

sources.note: Nothing about stress/accent. Sec. 1.1 (p. 89): Bobo is a lexical tone language with three level tones H, M, L plus contour tones (inventory of contours disputed between Morse 1976 and Le Bris & Prost 1981) and grammatical tone; the paper is an instrumental study of phrase-final F0, final lengthening and phonation with 3 speakers recorded in Bobo-Dioulasso 2013-14; 'prominence' is only mentioned as an elicitation target, no word-level prominence is described.
